Description.Summary: OpenAI Codex is OpenAI's AI coding agent (category: coding agent) that writes features, fixes bugs, answers codebase questions, reviews code and proposes pull requests. It ships on several platforms: the open-source, Rust-based Codex CLI that runs locally in the terminal (github.com/openai/codex), IDE extensions (VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf), a desktop app, and the cloud-based Codex web agent inside ChatGPT. Only some parts are open source: the CLI, SDK and app-server live in the public repository, while the IDE extension and Codex cloud are closed source.

evidence.quote: Codex CLI is a coding agent from OpenAI that runs locally on your computer.

Codex, which OpenAI launched in its modern incarnation as a research preview in May 2025, operates as a cloud-based software engineering agent that can handle tasks like writing features, fixing bugs, and proposing pull requests.
OpenAI develops key parts of Codex in the open. That work lives on GitHub so you can follow progress, report issues, and contribute improvements.
OpenAI had two teams tackle different segments of the problem space: Codex Web would focus on an async, cloud-based solution, while Codex CLI targeted iterative, local development.

Practices.Summary: The Codex team structures its codebase so that agents can check their own work. It keeps tests in place, clear module boundaries and explicit validation instructions, so a failing test tells the agent to retry. Codex has a dedicated skill for testing itself that runs the tests for all of Codex's own features. Nightly Codex runs look for issues across the codebase and leave suggested fixes for engineers to review in the morning.

evidence.quote: The team has deliberately structured their codebase “to make it inevitable for the model to succeed”.
Structuring means having tests in-place, clear module boundaries, and instructions on how the model should run validation (eg: tests, linting, etc).

The team set up nightly runs of Codex, instructed to look for issues across Codex.

Practices.Summary: Automated testing is split between pre-merge and post-merge. Required PR checks run against GitHub's synthetic merge commit. Bazel test and clippy are the main pre-merge path. The heavier Cargo nextest matrix (per-platform shards, including Windows ARM64), release-profile builds and Linux remote-env tests run after merge on main. nextest retries a failing test once, so transient failures do not fail full CI.

evidence.quote: Required checks run against GitHub's synthetic merge commit, not the pull request head alone.

The whole team runs bug-bash sessions: in one hour it logged and triaged more than 100 issues, and most were fixed within 24 hours. Before each launch, Codex is used to hunt for critical issues. The Codex app also runs through its own UI with skills, clicking around and attaching screenshot evidence to PRs, because end-to-end verification is becoming the bottleneck.

Others.Summary: Reliability is also built into language and code-review choices. Rust was picked partly for correctness (strong typing, memory management) and for a small dependency surface that the team can audit. The repository's review guideline asks for deep-equality assertions in tests and discourages `unsafe`; using `unsafe` std::env::set_var has caused race conditions more than once.

evidence.quote: For example, there are cases where it is tempting to use `unsafe` in order to use `std::env::set_var()`, but this indeed `unsafe` and has led to race conditions on multiple occasions.
We wanted to choose a language that helps eliminate a class of errors with things like strong typing and memory management.
By going with Rust, the team has very few dependencies and can thoroughly look through the few dependencies there are.

The split keeps PR signal fast while main still gets full cross-platform verification.

Issues.Issue_Title: bwrap: Approval prompt shown for almost every command
Issues.Description: After upgrading to CLI 0.115.0, the bubblewrap-based Linux sandbox asked for approval on almost every read-only command and did not save "don't ask again" decisions. Maintainers said the migration from Landlock to bubblewrap was complex and had introduced regressions, and fixed it in 0.122.0-alpha.9, a sign that changes to the security boundary are hard to roll out across Linux distributions.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug: Linux sandbox fails with mountinfo path is not absolute after ChatGPT update
Issues.Description: After a desktop update (bundled CLI 0.155.0-alpha.16), the Linux bubblewrap sandbox could not build its command because of an unexpected mountinfo path, so no commands could run. Sandbox setup depends on host-specific kernel and mount details that the test matrix does not fully cover.

Issues.Issue_Title: Codex reads files outside working directory without my permission
Issues.Description: A user found that the sandbox restricts writes but not reads outside the working directory. A maintainer explained this is by design (tools need read access) and pointed to a feature request for finer-grained policies. Users' expectations of the security model did not match its default enforcement.

Issues.Issue_Title: [CRITICAL DATA LOSS][Windows] Codex mass-deleted hundreds of GB outside project scope, including unrelated projects, apps and Windows components
Issues.Description: A destructive filesystem operation on Windows reportedly escaped the project scope and deleted user data, applications and OS components. This is a safety-critical gap in containing destructive tool calls, especially on Windows, where the sandbox has fewer OS primitives.

Issues.Issue_Title: Windows sandbox provisioning fails with os error 32 when any runtime file is in use (0.162.0-alpha.2 regression)
Issues.Description: A new runtime validation step in the 0.162.0-alpha.2 Windows sandbox helper aborts provisioning whenever a runtime file is open by a running process. As a result, every sandboxed command in the desktop app is rejected, an example of an alpha-channel regression in Windows-specific sandbox code.

Issues.Issue_Title: Codex SQLite feedback logs can write ~640 TB/year and rapidly consume SSD endurance
Issues.Description: Codex's local SQLite feedback log database (~/.codex/logs_2.sqlite) logged every Responses WebSocket event, which caused extreme disk writes. A maintainer fixed it in several PRs released in 0.142.0–0.145.0. This was unbounded local telemetry that no performance test caught before release.

Issues.Issue_Title: MCP server processes leak: per-thread processes never cleaned up (9+ GB RSS)
Issues.Description: The app-server starts a full set of MCP server processes for every thread and never stops them when threads close. In the report, 133 orphaned processes were using about 9.3 GB of RAM, which shows gaps in process lifecycle management in the multi-thread app-server design.

Issues.Issue_Title: unexpected status 404 Not Found: Unknown error, url: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses, cf-ray: ...
Issues.Description: Long-running sessions with compaction and sub-agents kept failing with 404s from the Codex backend Responses endpoint after 5 retries. With more than 1,100 comments, it shows how client failures depend on backend and model-routing behavior outside the open-source repository.

Issues.Issue_Title: WebSocket upgrade succeeds then server closes with 1008 Policy (falls back to HTTPS)
Issues.Description: The new Responses WebSocket transport was closed right away by server policy, which caused reconnect loops and fallback to HTTPS. Maintainers debugged it with logs and thread IDs uploaded through /feedback, a client/server transport contract issue in a feature-flagged rollout.

Issues.Issue_Title: Codex Desktop GPT-5.5 remote compaction fails and leaves thread unusable
Issues.Description: Automatic remote context compaction failed with stream disconnects and left threads stuck. The team fixed it architecturally by moving compaction logic to the client and using the same endpoint as normal turns, replacing a separate server-side endpoint.

Issues.Issue_Title: Codex App: context compaction fails with invalid_enum_value for `context_compaction`
Issues.Description: After compaction, the client sent an item type that the Responses API schema rejected (invalid_enum_value). It was closed as a duplicate of related schema-mismatch reports, part of a recurring class of API contract and schema drift between the client and the backend.

Issues.Issue_Title: codex app-server can pollute subsequent TUI session metadata (wrong cwd/source/originator)
Issues.Description: Running `codex app-server` caused later TUI sessions to be recorded with the wrong working directory, source and originator in rollout files and the SQLite state DB. It was fixed in 0.133.0. Shared local state between surfaces (CLI, app-server, desktop) is a source of cross-surface bugs.

Right after the 0.124.0 release, npm installs failed because the platform-specific optional package was missing; a maintainer said npm uploads may not have finished yet. This is a packaging and publishing race in the multi-package npm distribution.

Issues.Issue_Title: [BUG] Codex CLI 0.157.0 fails to start on Windows with daemon privilege error (0.156.1 works)
Issues.Description: A new background-daemon privilege check in 0.157.0 made the CLI fail at startup on Windows with an error saying the daemon must be started from a non-elevated terminal. Downgrading to 0.156.1 avoided it. A new architectural component (the shared app-server daemon) caused a platform-specific startup regression.

Issues.Issue_Title: Linux arm64: bundled codex-linux-arm64 musl binary segfaults with SEGV_ACCERR (exit 139)
Issues.Description: The bundled MUSL-linked arm64 binary crashes with SIGSEGV on Raspberry Pi/aarch64 Linux. Shipping statically linked binaries for every target leaves gaps in coverage of less common architectures.

Practices.Summary: The selected issues fall into four recurring categories. (1) Sandbox and security-boundary regressions across OS backends: the Linux migration to bubblewrap, Windows sandbox helpers, and read-scope expectations. (2) Unbounded resource growth and leaks: SQLite log writes, orphaned MCP processes, and session-history scans. (3) Client/backend transport and schema contract mismatches: Responses API 404s, WebSocket policy closes, remote-compaction failures, enum/schema drift, and shared app-server state polluting other surfaces. (4) Release and packaging regressions from a very fast release cadence: missing npm optional packages, MUSL arm64 segfaults, and the Windows daemon privilege error. Together they point to a weak spot: one shared harness ships to many surfaces and platforms faster than cross-platform tests can cover. Maintainers usually respond with quick alpha or point-release fixes, and sometimes with architectural changes such as moving compaction to the client.

evidence.quote: We have a complex migration underway and it seems like it introduced regressions.
We recently switched to a more robust approach where the compaction logic is moved locally using the same endpoint as normal turns.
Our series of fixes for this problem are in the latest shipping desktop app, CLI, and IDE extension.

Practices.Summary: The team works in the open on Slack. At OpenAI almost everything runs on Slack rather than email. The Codex team deliberately uses public channels and open documents with broad permissions, and Codex is connected to Slack, documents and code, so anyone can ask it who is working on what or why a decision was made.

Practices.Summary: Meetings are few and spontaneous. The team favors in-person collaboration, and leadership is very available. In meetings, engineers often start a Codex thread to answer questions on the spot.

Practices.Summary: Onboarding uses pairing. A new joiner shadows an engineer for the first half of the day, then gets a task to ship to production the same day. Codex also walks new hires through setup and the codebase.

Practices.Summary: Written artifacts are part of the engineering process. PR bodies must explain the motivation for the change, and unit tests are seen as "executable documentation". OpenAI engineers stress producing artifacts that humans enjoy reading because the same artifacts make agents more reliable.
